title: A FIRE SHUT UP IN MY BONES : THE WORK THE ZEAL THE FIRE

sense.text:
“His word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones.” That is how this Bible needs to be for us: the word burning in our hearts, and not only burning but shut up in the bones. When you feel something deep in your bones it is inescapable. It is not surface level. It is not something we do; it is who we are.

“And I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.” In this moment Jeremiah felt like giving up, but the word always wins, and it would not let him give up.

Brothers and sisters talk about being tired and weary, and brothers misuse battle fatigue. The Bishop taught battle fatigue and it went over everybody’s head: battle fatigue really means sin is winning, your flesh beating you up so you don’t want to keep these laws anymore. Most of the men who say they are battle fatigued are just lazy. No passion, no fire. That is why all the excuses abound.

We have to have the mind and spirit of Christ, and here is what moved him: “when he saw the multitudes, he was moved with compassion on them.” Verse 35 says he was teaching in their synagogues, so these are Israelites. It is not compassion on the whole world, but on his people, because he will save his people from their sins, which is us.

“Because they fainted.” Think about how they fainted: alcoholism, drugs, whoremongers, fornicators, men not taking care of their families, lost in Christianity, lost in politics. When you are not living your true heritage you have fainted, because the real you is not alive, not conscious. Satan is in the driver’s seat.

“As sheep having no shepherd.” Christ saw a void of teachers and leaders with fire in their bones to teach their people the right thing, and he was moved with compassion.

Compassion is a feeling of deep sympathy and sorrow for another who is stricken by misfortune, accompanied by a strong desire to alleviate the suffering. The misfortune is the curses we are under. Deep sympathy and sorrow is them that sigh and cry in Ezekiel for the abominations they saw our people in, and Paul in Romans 9 wishing he could be accursed for what his people would go through. But compassion is more than sympathy. It compels you to do something for the stricken. Sympathy alone does nothing, like saying be warm and filled and never giving the food or the clothing. Hold on to that, because compassion is not far off from the fire that gets in your bones.

Our people are so lacking in compassion for their own that they are quicker to defend other nations; that is hatred for your brother. Sayings like don’t forget where you came from, and you can’t rise above the condition of your people, exist because of that lack of compassion.

“The harvest truly is plenteous, but the labourers are few.” We quote this a lot without thinking about what prompted him to say it. Compassion for our people is what should drive us to be laborers. There are so many of us, and a great work to gather our people, to help alleviate their misfortune, the curses, and to bring them light in the dark place where they reside.
“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.” This is the call to labor that the rest of the class builds on.

“Get wisdom, get understanding: forget it not.” You come in, you repent, you get wisdom and understanding, and then the scripture says forget it not, letting you know that things have to happen for you to retain it or you will lose it. It is like starting a new job or starting school: excited at first, and six months later you hate it, because of the pull of other things in the world.

It is not difficult to keep the commandments; it is written plainly what to do and not do. Christianity goes to great lengths to defend not keeping the law, even while agreeing it is wrong to rape, fornicate, rob and steal. You keep the law every day you don’t do those things. There is a spirit in man that prevents him from embracing that.

“Neither decline from the words of my mouth.” He just told you how you don’t forget it: you stay in these scriptures and meditate on them. Not to decline means not to faint, to stay consistent in keeping these laws.

“Forsake her not, and she shall preserve thee: love her, and she shall keep thee. Wisdom is the principal thing.” Wisdom is the foundation of everything, and the foundation of how you build that fire in your bones.

“With all thy getting get understanding.” Knowledge is opening the book and learning that the Sabbath is the seventh day, keep it, wear your fringes. Wisdom is actually doing it, and never ceasing, never declining from doing it. Understanding does not come until you grow to wisdom.

Getting wisdom takes effort; it is not passive. “Seek ye out of the book of the Lord, and read.” To seek is to go in search or quest, to try to find or discover by searching or questioning. Seeking the Bible should gender questions. When brothers have no questions, they are not reading and not applying. Nobody has taught this Bible cover to cover the way the Israelites are teaching it now, so there is always something to uncover.

“No one of these shall fail.” Not one precept fails, and keeping the commandments benefits you, however hard people fight to defend not keeping them. “His spirit it hath gathered them” is the spirit of Christ, and it is God’s spirit harvesting and gathering his people when we do this work.

Seeking is not just for knowledge. It is seeking to build yourself in the spirit of compassion, compelled to help, with fire in your bones to build. If grudges, personal sin and your opinions of others are still stumbling blocks for you, you don’t have it yet. Stick your nose back in there and seek some more.

We need to seek, learn and labor, in that order. The more we grow in wisdom, the more able we are to teach, correct and lead our people. Knowledge without zeal is stagnation. Zeal without wisdom becomes misdirection: willing brothers without a foundation of wisdom, like them that teach the milk and are unskillful in the word. Knowledge needs zeal, zeal leads to wisdom, and together they make you effective.

Up to this point Jeremiah had been warning of the judgment of the Most High and blasting Judah for their treachery and corruption. Everybody wants to blame the northern kingdom, as if the southern kingdom did not do the same or worse. Judah saw what happened to the northern kingdom and still did it, which makes them worse, because they knew better.

“Now Pashur the son of Immer the priest, who was also chief governor in the house of the Lord, heard that Jeremiah prophesied these things”: the wars and the judgment that Jeremiah prophesied against their wickedness.

“Then Pashur smote Jeremiah the prophet”: he beat him up, just for prophesying the truth, “and put him in the stocks that were in the high gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the Lord.”

The stocks held him twisted up with his head locked in, and they were set in a public place so that everybody could shame him: throwing things at him, cursing him, spitting on him, and he could do nothing. That is done to break a man’s spirit. Examine yourself: is anything you are dealing with strong enough to break your spirit and fire for the Lord? The answer should be unequivocally hell no.

“The Lord hath not called thy name Pashur, but Magor–missabib.” Magor–missabib means fear round about, which is why he says “I will make thee a terror to thyself.” The stocks did not break Jeremiah’s spirit. He came out emboldened and cursed him.

Jeremiah had no power to “give all Judah into the hand of the king of Babylon.” That is the spirit of the Lord speaking through him: Pashur, his house and all his friends to whom he had prophesied lies would go into captivity and die in Babylon, and Judah with them.

Verses 7 onward show where Jeremiah’s spirit was while he was locked up in the stocks, communing with the Lord.

“O Lord, thou hast deceived me, and I was deceived.” He is not saying God lied to him. He did not realize how powerful his calling would be: that after being beaten and put in the stocks he would come out wanting to preach the word all the more. It is like the apostles who rejoiced when they came out of prison because they had been afflicted for Christ’s name, and it made them more zealous. That is a unique spirit, and not everybody has it.

“Thou art stronger than I, and hast prevailed.” He was ready to give up and considered it in his mind, but the fire the Lord put in him took him to another level.

“For since I spake, I cried out, I cried violence and spoil”: what he prophesied against Judah. “Because the word of the Lord was made a reproach unto me, and a derision, daily.” Every time he spoke the word he was cursed out, spit on, beaten, chased out of town and thrown in the stocks.

“Then I said, I will not make mention of him, nor speak any more in his name.” He considered not prophesying anymore, like brothers and sisters who say they have to get right before they come back, as if you can get right without the word.

“But his word was in mine heart as a burning fire shut up in my bones.” Verse 7 is explained in verse 9: he was deceived because he did not realize how powerful the word was in him. The spirit is stronger than the flesh.

“I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay”: weary of trying not to do the Lord’s will. He does not mean he wanted to give up; he means, I am tired of fighting you, God; you are stronger than me. Something is shut up inside him, and the spirit will not let him rest until he speaks. If you have never felt that, where you have to say something to rebuke and correct a spirit and bring the edification out, you are not where you need to be yet in this walk.

Compulsion is a strong, usually irresistible impulse to perform an act, especially one contrary to one’s will. In the flesh Jeremiah had every right to give up, but that compulsion would not let him. The fire conquers weariness. With it you will never have battle fatigue and never think of walking away, even when people you love walk away. Your salvation is not tied to anybody else; it is built on this word and on Christ.

If his word is truly in your heart, it will burn until you speak it. There is never a time when there is nothing to talk about in the scriptures; it should always be a discovery.

“I heard the defaming of many, fear on every side.” “All my familiars watched for my halting, saying, Peradventure he will be enticed, and we shall prevail against him, and we shall take our revenge on him.” These are the things he was dealing with.

“But the Lord is with me as a mighty terrible one: therefore my persecutors shall stumble, and they shall not prevail.” Here he explains what he reasoned out in the stocks. He is encouraging himself, building himself up, feeding the fire he has from the Lord. “For unto thee have I opened my cause.”

“Sing unto the Lord, praise ye the Lord: for he hath delivered the soul of the poor from the hand of evildoers.” His struggle turns to praise because he realizes his purpose. Knowing there is a God and that redemption waits on the other side, whatever you are afflicted with, is what built him up.

This is the cost of conviction. For some of us it will literally happen again; you see shades of it in the travels and in how people attack us. That inescapable drive makes you run toward danger, like the man who runs into a burning building to save someone, and that is compassion again. It shows you are a real one, a true servant, not a fair-weather friend who stops being a friend in times of difficulty. Imagine having to gather in secret upon pain of death like our forefathers, when some cannot even make it in when they are depressed.

precepts.why:
Purpose is the reason for which something exists or is done, and Jeremiah knew his. “Before I formed thee in the belly I knew thee”: God knew his soul and his spirit. “And before thou camest forth out of the womb I sanctified thee, and I ordained thee a prophet unto the nations.”

That was his purpose, and it stayed with him through everything he went through. To realize you have been called to something higher is what turns weariness into praise. Until you have graduated to purpose in this, you are just spending your time here, deciding by emotion and rationalizing after the fact.

Jeremiah went through all of it and realized there is something inside him that will never stop, and if it means he dies doing it, so be it. Purpose conquers weariness. We are going to get the reproach, but face it head on with zeal, trusting that the Most High is always faithful to his laborers.

A different example of the burning in the heart. “Did not our heart burn within us, while he talked with us by the way, and while he opened to us the scriptures?” This is when the disciples saw Christ. He opened their understanding and they saw the prophecies fulfilled in him, and it lit something in them: a yearning, a compulsion, a compassion that moves you.

It is the same burning Jeremiah felt, but Jeremiah’s came through affliction, and this came through understanding and revelation. Jeremiah’s fire was the compulsion to speak truth despite suffering, growing stronger the more he suffered; the disciples’ was awareness and joy at things being revealed. You need both.

Most people have the Luke kind for a season: a class comes out and it was fire. But when the word is truly received, it ignites a purpose for a mission inside you. When your heart burns from the word, your mouth must open to teach it from understanding, and when you go through things it should pull you back to your purpose so you move forward and share it.

sense.text:
Why does he call it a harvest? Because our purpose is to gather our people through his spirit, the spirit that gathered them in Isaiah 34. Just as God foreknew Jeremiah as a prophet to his people, he uses us to gather his people.

Gathering is not only everybody on the front line bringing people in. It also means keeping the same energy and zeal in the body. If people come in and see disorganization and strife not being addressed, the gathering fails. A congregation is like an emergency room: you will see sick people, but you should see treatment happening, not sickness fostered and allowed to grow. People have to be brought into something so they are filled with purpose, not just attendance.

It is like an ecosystem: everything relies on something else, and if the smallest part collapses, the whole thing collapses. From the brother who takes the trash cans out, to the one who lines up the chairs, to the one directing parking, if one is not in place we lose the effect of gathering. Many brothers are excited about teaching but not about anything else once the people are here, and one should not exist without the other.

To harvest is to gather, and you have to gather into a system. A fisherman who casts his net and leaves the fish rotting on the boat, never bringing them to shore or feeding the village, wasted his fishing. You have to be as on fire for those other layers as you are compelled to speak the word, though it starts with the compulsion to teach.

“Pray ye therefore the Lord of the harvest, that he will send forth labourers into his harvest.” You don’t just pray for it; in those prayers you are saying you will put your hand to the plow to help bring those laborers about, develop the men and bring something out.

Malcolm X, in his autobiography, had this same spirit Christ had when he saw them without a shepherd. He thought it outrageous that his small temple still had empty seats with the surrounding streets full of brainwashed brothers and sisters (insert fainted from verse 36) drinking, cursing, fighting and using dope. He called the recruitment attitude a self-defeating waiting view, the assumption that God would just bring more in. There should be no empty seats. The sisters’ response to everything on the internet is freaking twerking: you messed up my order, I’m going to twerk; you spoke to me nasty, I’m going to twerk. It’s disgusting, and that is the state of our people.

When we gather people into groups and only answer questions, we are not recruiting. Gathering is recruiting, like a military recruiter who stays on your ass until you enlist because he knows something will pull you away. We don’t want dead weight or seat warmers, on the brothers’ side or the sisters’.

The New York captains spoke of the same thing: why people have no sense of urgency, especially here in the West. Picture somebody chilling in slides or chanclas; you can’t hustle in slides, they fall off. That is the mentality, and not only in the West.

When we pray for more laborers, it is not only new people; it is the brothers and sisters already here maturing enough to put in the work. Where the hell are you? Especially you men: when are you going to get all your namby-pamby BS behind you and get the spirit of Jeremiah and the spirit of the disciples, so that we can gather more? Not ideas; anybody can get ideas. Brothers with zeal, fire, wisdom, purpose and compassion. God will not give the increase if he does not see us ready to facilitate the growth. Paul planted, Apollos watered, God gave the increase, but the work still has to be done. The three thousand souls in one day will come when we have the attitude right and the fire surging through each of us.

Malcolm said he had been impatient, and that is the spirit of Bishop Nathaniel from the beginning: not irrationally, but because of compassion and zeal that never ceases. We have a great cloud of witnesses in the scriptures and in our leaders. Some senior women have that fire too; sisters play a strong supportive role and should covet earnestly those desires, but far too few have it, and the same on the men’s side. Think of the white supremacist movements: those white women support the evil they do wholeheartedly. They are not lying in the cut doing nothing, quarreling among themselves; they have that same fire and zeal for wickedness. When are we going to see that with our sisters?

precepts.why:
Harvest literally means to gather the crops. “Gather yourselves together, yea, gather together, O nation not desired.” The nation not desired goes into Christ’s compassion on those that fainted and had no shepherd, stricken with misfortune.

“Before the decree bring forth, before the day pass as the chaff.” It keeps the language of the harvest. Chaff is the husk of grains and grasses separated during threshing. To pass as the chaff is to be destroyed, tossed to the side as good for nothing. That speaks first of the other nations and of those of our people that follow behind them and don’t repent before Christ returns, “before the fierce anger of the Lord come upon you, before the day of the Lord’s anger come upon you.”

But gathered into what? We have to be gathered under structure and all the things we are doing. You don’t just gather together and wait.

sense.text: “I will not be burdensome to you: for I seek not yours, but you.” This is the spirit we must have. Many of us deceive ourselves that we are fervent in spirit, the way people lie to themselves that they are in a calorie deficit while the scale never budges. Anybody who has been an activist or revolutionary has this drive, and ours should be bolder and grander because we have the sure word: none of these shall fail.

“I will very gladly spend and be spent for you.” To spend is to use up, consume or exhaust, and to give one’s blood, life and so on for some cause. Paul is willing to exhaust and consume himself for compassion on his people. That is the impatience and drive, not the self-defeating attitude of just waiting on the Lord to give the increase.

Many brothers say they would die for you, take a bullet, but cannot put in the effort to be spent for their people in the day-to-day work. To be spent means there is nothing left. The longer, slower death is giving your blood and life by devoting your life to the Lord in Christ, and so to your brothers and sisters and your people, choosing every moment to let that fire reign. You may get frustrated, vexed and annoyed dealing with Israel, but never tired of fulfilling your purpose.

“Though the more abundantly I love you, the less I be loved.” The more he pours himself into his people, the less he is appreciated; they mumble that he is too burdensome, too intense, not brotherly. But if a child is about to put a knife in an outlet, or a brother stands in front of a bus, you tackle him and hurt yourselves in the process to save him. There is a war and a mission here.

The margin of some Bibles reads your souls. It is not the carnal brother or sister he is spent for, but the soul and spirit inside. We perceive things earthly, but we have to move spiritually.

precepts.why:
Same theme. “Obey them that have the rule over you, and submit yourselves: for they watch for your souls.” Submit means do what is being taught and apply it. Paul gladly spends himself for their souls, and here the rulers watch for their souls.

“As they that must give account, that they may do it with joy, and not with grief: for that is unprofitable for you.” The more I love you, the less I am loved, but in rebelling you are only being unprofitable for yourself, because the leader must give account for your soul. The Lord will ask a leader about every member, man, woman and child: why didn’t you take the oversight, why didn’t you notice this. That is why there is anger at those with no sense of urgency in developing the brothers and sisters.

Laborers are not only for the streets; they are needed to build the men that are here. It is easier to bring fruit from a tree already planted than to wait on a seedling, though both must be done. We all have jobs, businesses, spouses, but never the attitude of I’m going to do me and the hell with everything else. It is called priorities. When it says with joy and not with grief, it goes back to Corinthians: you make it grievous and unjoyful to help you.

sense.text: “For whosoever shall call upon the name of the Lord shall be saved.” With the calling comes application and learning. It makes no sense that you just call something out and receive it. You call out your order at a pizza shop and don’t pay, he takes the pizza back. You can’t stand in a car dealership, say Honda Civic, and drive off the lot; there is paperwork, license, registration. We understand it in carnal things, but in spiritual things we get stupid.

“How then shall they call on him in whom they have not believed? and how shall they believe in him of whom they have not heard? and how shall they hear without a preacher? And how shall they preach, except they be sent?” How can they call on him if we don’t have the fire to go out and do the gathering? “How beautiful are the feet of them that preach the gospel of peace.”

“But they have not all obeyed the gospel.” Calling is tied to obeying. What is written in the New Testament is also the commandments of the Lord, as Paul says, and the point is obedience. “Lord, who hath believed our report?” Belief is demonstrated by action.
“So then faith cometh by hearing, and hearing by the word of God.” We must keep the fire in us to labor for God and our people, so that they can hear.
“Give attendance to reading, to exhortation, to doctrine.” These are the foundations of what we do to keep the fire roaring inside us.

“Neglect not the gift that is in thee.” That neglect is what we all do. Some don’t yet know what gift is in them. We all have at least the gift of receiving this word; many of our people will fight to the death to say they are Gentiles and not Israelites, and that alone should move you with compassion and frustration, not at them but at where their minds are. Beyond that there are diversities of gifts. Don’t you want to know your role and purpose?

“With the laying on of the hands of the presbytery.” The presbytery is the elders of the church. Laying on of hands is not only healing; it is the elders setting men in positions and praying over them, as when captains and up are promoted and anointed, called into something greater by God through those men.

“Meditate upon these things; give thyself wholly to them.” This is the part we all miss: one foot in and one foot out. If the fire is foreign to you, you have not given yourself wholly. In the stocks is when Jeremiah gave himself wholly; he stopped resisting.

In basic training the TI told the recruits they sucked because they were resisting what they were trying to make them, and until they stopped resisting they would keep sucking and some would not make it. Once you embrace it and give yourself wholly, it is still demanding, but you are no longer fighting it. Those still holding on to all their BS trivial things have not given themselves wholly. Take a moral inventory of your desires and ask whether you have given yourself wholly to God and to this mission.

“That thy profiting may appear to all”: not for selfish reasons, but for all.

“Take heed unto thyself, and unto the doctrine; continue in them: for in doing this thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.” That is the fire inside. When you commit this way you not only save yourself, you become profitable for your people. It is two things we must focus on.

precepts.why:
An example of the laying on of hands. “And the saying pleased the whole multitude: and they chose Stephen, a man full of faith and of the Holy Ghost,” with Philip, Prochorus, Nicanor, Timon, Parmenas and Nicolas. They brought out understanding and preached, as in Romans 10, and then chose out certain men.

“Whom they set before the apostles”: the apostles were the presbytery, the chief ones. “And when they had prayed, they laid their hands on them.” They were given an assignment and a purpose, just as God chose Jeremiah and gave him a mission. In these days certain people are called and given their purpose the same way.

“And the word of God increased; and the number of the disciples multiplied in Jerusalem greatly.” Why did they multiply greatly? Because it was about gathering: they kept looking for others to put to work, hands to the plow, filled with fire. “And a great company of the priests were obedient to the faith.”

“But the manifestation of the Spirit is given to every man to profit withal.” When you give yourself wholly, that manifestation of the spirit is given to each of us. What we read in Jeremiah 20 and Luke 24 was that manifestation for those men in that moment.

Jeremiah was preaching all along and still, unknown to us, often contemplated not doing it anymore. In the stocks he gave himself wholly: there is something in me that prevents me from doing anything else with my life, and even knowing I will die doing this, I cannot resist it. That is the profiting that appears to all.

“The wisdom of a learned man cometh by opportunity of leisure: and he that hath little business shall become wise.” To give yourself wholly you have to prioritize what is really important to you. When brothers are exhorted they rattle off the list of all their responsibilities in the world. Nobody cares: not insensitively, but those excuses are lies.

It does not mean you do one and not the other; you can do both. “How can he get wisdom that holdeth the plough, and that glorieth in the goad, that driveth oxen, and is occupied in their labours, and whose talk is of bullocks?” Unless you make the effort to give yourself to this. When all you talk about is everything else in your life, you are saying loudly, I’m not really about this yet.

You want to be part of this on your time, your conditions and your schedule. Nobody is told to quit their job; find a way. Where your treasure is, there your heart is, and this has not become your treasure yet. You are not ready to spend and be spent.

“Consider that I laboured not for myself only, but for all them that seek learning.” It is the same as “thou shalt both save thyself, and them that hear thee.” Many think they are here only for their own salvation. Yes, you stand alone and seek your own, but you also seek for others. That is the duality: all of us putting ourselves on the line for each other. That is fire, intensity, zeal and passion, and it will take us to the next level.

Something big is on the horizon. The internet gave us exposure the news could not black out; influencers and podcasts have overtaken the news, and anything Israelite is portrayed as purple and gold. Whether it is twelve schools in a new country or three thousand souls in one day, more challenges and afflictions will come with it, and we must be prepared. “For all them that seek learning”: our people are thirsty and hungry for it.

sense.text: “Need we, as some others, epistles of commendation to you, or letters of commendation from you?” Commendation is like merit and praise: do we need you to tell us how great we are, how fire the class was? Say it if you are compelled, but it is not a necessity.

“Ye are our epistle written in our hearts, known and read of all men.” What we need from you is to replicate what we are doing. We have fire, you have fire; we teach, gather and build, you teach, gather and build. That makes you the letter of commendation. Our success is measured in you, not in numbers but in the quality of the behavior and the consistency and longevity of what is put forth. One day the corporation on paper won’t exist, but we are not going anywhere.

“Written not with ink, but with the Spirit of the living God”: that spirit entering each one of us. “Not in tables of stone, but in fleshy tables of the heart”: because you see action and movement behind it. The fleshy heart goes into behaviors.
“And such trust have we through Christ to God-ward.” That is the confidence that comes from seeing those things in the people.

“Not of the letter, but of the spirit: for the letter killeth, but the spirit giveth life.” Scoffers will seize on this as if it means not keeping the law. The whole point of reading it is the epistle: we need to replicate that fire and zeal, and part of the work is having others do the same.

precepts.why:
“Through this man is preached unto you the forgiveness of sins”: through Christ. “And by him all that believe are justified from all things, from which ye could not be justified by the law of Moses.”

It is plain to be understood. The judgment for the sins is crucified with Christ; the law of Moses could not justify us. How Christians get from that to not keeping the commandments makes no sense.

Think of the fleshy heart and what it represents. “This is the covenant that I will make with the house of Israel after those days, saith the Lord; I will put my laws into their mind, and write them in their hearts: and I will be to them a God, and they shall be to me a people.”

Written in the fleshy tables of the heart means that we do them: the laws are still present, and they are what we are guided by. The laws, the word, are ultimately that fire, and there are tangible things we can do to light it or make it the roaring fire inside you that you can’t contain.

sense.text: Now the pursuit of wisdom and understanding, the part of Proverbs 4 that says get wisdom, get understanding, and of Isaiah 34 that says seek. “Ask, and it shall be given you; seek, and ye shall find; knock, and it shall be opened unto you.” As the horse is prepared for battle but safety is of the Lord, we put forth the effort and then wisdom and understanding are given. “For every one that asketh receiveth; and he that seeketh findeth.”

“If his son ask bread, will he give him a stone?” This is the spirit the Father and Christ move in: he will not give you something contrary to what is needful. You want to be like Jeremiah, the disciples, Paul, Christ? He will give it to you, but you have to show him you are ready to give yourself wholly. If it has not been given, it is because you are still double minded and unstable. “How much more shall your Father which is in heaven give good things to them that ask him?”

“All things whatsoever ye would that men should do to you, do ye even so to them: for this is the law and the prophets.” Christianity takes this as do unto others. We apply the royal law, but this really goes into 1 Timothy 4:16: by giving yourself wholly you save yourself and others. We build ourselves so we can build others, with that recruitment mentality, so others come behind us as living epistles, keeping the new covenant with fleshy hearts.

precepts.why:
Christ talks about knocking and seeking, and here he says he is the one knocking and waiting. “Behold, I stand at the door, and knock: if any man hear my voice, and open the door.” To open the door means saying, I will do what you say. Notice the action, like the pizza and the car: not calling on the name of the Lord and nothing else. If you never open the door, you cannot receive what is at the door.

“I will come in to him, and will sup with him, and he with me.” That is what we desire. Christ finds you and calls you; you have to open the door and seek to keep him present with you, because the Holy Spirit won’t dwell in a malicious soul. This is part of with all thy getting get understanding.

sense.text: “If thou wilt receive my words, and hide my commandments with thee”: receive the word, hear the call, hide his commandments with you. Open the door and let him in.
“So that thou incline thine ear unto wisdom, and apply thine heart to understanding.” To incline your ear is to say, I need to hear that, and then you apply yourself to understanding.

“If thou criest after knowledge, and liftest up thy voice for understanding” is another precept of calling upon him. “If thou seekest her as silver”: seek and you shall find, knock and the door will open. “And searchest for her as for hid treasures.” Many of us have not gone to that extent. Seek it out does not just mean buy a Bible and follow along in class. The way you know you must eat and drink and don’t feel right without it, the way some need their coffee every day, that is how you look for this. It is the apple of your eye.

“Then shalt thou understand the fear of the Lord.” Then, after you have done all these things. You have not understood the fear of the Lord if you have not done them. “And find the knowledge of God.” Seek, then understand; from understanding comes fear, and knowledge follows after. Knowledge is not just knowing the precept. The fear of the Lord is the entry-level requirement for knowledge: if you fear God, you won’t do things contrary to what he says.
“For the Lord giveth wisdom: out of his mouth cometh knowledge and understanding.” The same as Matthew 7 and Revelation 3: insight into what you need to do to build that fire inside of you.

“If thou wilt, thou shalt be taught: and if thou wilt apply thy mind, thou shalt be prudent. If thou love to hear, thou shalt receive understanding.” “Stand in the multitude of the elders; and cleave unto him that is wise.” These are the steps for building yourself in understanding.

“Be willing to hear every godly discourse; and let not the parables of understanding escape thee.” Brothers say they want every godly discourse, and it is a lie. They mean precepts for their notes. But when the spirit moves on a high holy day and you are called out, corrected and admonished, you don’t want to hear it and you don’t apply it. That is godly discourse too. You stand among the elders and you get called out, and you leave saying you were abused.

The brother who never takes accountability keeps going through the same thing, prays for judgment against the brothers who judged him, fasts for the leaders to change instead of himself. Then he avoids the table and sits in the back, Bible open with nothing on the page, talking to Satan in his head. The joy of the Lord is supposed to be your strength.

“If thou seest a man of understanding, get thee betimes unto him.” Brothers apply that only when they want their questions answered, not when they have things they can’t get over. Tell a brother what you see in his spirit and he gives you the stupid face; eight brothers tell him the same thing and now they are all conspiring against him. “And let thy foot wear the steps of his door.”

“Let thy mind be upon the ordinances of the Lord”: the law written in your fleshy heart. “And meditate continually in his commandments”: give yourself wholly. “He shall establish thine heart”: he will set your purpose and light that fire. “And give thee wisdom at thine owns desire.” If you are not growing or being promoted, it is because none of this is being received and applied.

“If any of you lack wisdom, let him ask of God, that giveth to all men liberally, and upbraideth not.” It is not difficult to get wisdom; it is abundantly there. Like an all-you-can-eat buffet, there is so much that people grow cold to it. Whatever the topic, it has been taught, probably by several teachers. Scarcity drives demand, and in our carnality the abundance of understanding is not appreciated. Man shall not live by bread alone: feed your spirit as much as your body. Some of you should miss a meal or two, but your spirit should never go without.

“But let him ask in faith, nothing wavering. For he that wavereth is like a wave of the sea driven with the wind and tossed.” That is double-mindedness, not asking right: not receiving the godly discourse, praying and applying it correctly. “For let not that man think that he shall receive any thing of the Lord.”

“A double minded man is unstable in all his ways.” Go back to Jeremiah 20: you are stronger than me, I grow weary of forbearing. That is the double-mindedness. Jeremiah acknowledged the instability, killed it and put it aside after the stocks: the fire in me is stronger than my own desires and will.

Until you examine yourself and purge out the instability, you will keep asking why you are not promoted, why you were demoted and not brought back. Maybe because you hate your brothers, or you are an emotional mess. The answer is in you. Unstable in all their ways: they can’t hold a job, they are always broke, always going back to their BS. That is the classic sign of the double minded. I’m on fire for this truth. No, you’re not.

Discipline, purpose and vision are the bridges to the fire, built on the foundation already laid. “Forgetting those things which are behind, and reaching forth unto those things which are before.” This is Paul, and we know how he dealt with his people before. Had he kept beating himself up over it, he could never have been on fire enough to say he would gladly spend and be spent. He put it behind him and used it as fuel to seek the Lord ten times more. That is singleness of mind, not double-mindedness, and how he endured all the afflictions he boasted of. It takes a magnanimous spirit.

“I press toward the mark for the prize of the high calling of God in Christ Jesus.” That is discipline, purpose and vision. That is how you put things behind you: without a vision in front of you, you look backwards. Put something in place to look forward to.

“He that giveth his mind to the law of the most High”: always giving, always wholly, submitted. “And is occupied in the meditation thereof, will seek out the wisdom of all the ancient.” There is that word seek again.
“He will keep the sayings of the renowned men”: keep them, not just hear them. To keep means to apply. “And where subtil parables are, he will be there also.”
“He will seek out the secrets of grave sentences, and be conversant in dark parables.” These are things you can do to build yourself, establishing discipline, purpose and vision.

“This book of the law shall not depart out of thy mouth; but thou shalt meditate therein day and night”: give yourself wholly to it. “That thou mayest observe to do”: the same as keeping the sayings of the renowned men in Ecclesiasticus 39. “For then thou shalt make thy way prosperous, and then thou shalt have good success”: then you will be filled with fire and have the vision to press forward.

“Be strong and of a good courage; be not afraid, neither be thou dismayed: for the Lord thy God is with thee whithersoever thou goest.” Jeremiah and Paul surely thought on these words in what they went through. The scriptures only truly sustain you when you remove the double-mindedness, discipline yourself and understand you were called to more. If you think you are here only for yourself, you will never rise to the level of our forefathers and mothers.
“That ye present your bodies a living sacrifice, holy, acceptable unto God”: again, give yourself wholly.

“And be not conformed to this world.” This is how you enable your discipline, purpose and vision: stop letting this world dictate them, stop acting carnal. “But be ye transformed by the renewing of your mind, that ye may prove what is that good, and acceptable, and perfect, will of God.” The only way is to be transformed in your mind.

We must have faithfulness and endure through trials. “Count it all joy when ye fall into divers temptations; Knowing this, that the trying of your faith worketh patience.” Was Jeremiah’s faith not tried at the outset of what he went through? Big time. And he was found acceptable and worthy, acknowledged his calling as a prophet, and had that fire in his bones.
“But let patience have her perfect work, that ye may be perfect and entire, wanting nothing.” This is the faithful part, read with the verses on wisdom and wavering that follow.

Now what the fire really is, and how everything before builds to it so you can maintain it. “I will make my words in thy mouth fire, and this people wood, and it shall devour them.” God empowers the true servant, the prophet, the true laborer, so that when he speaks the word it acts with a consuming power.

Like the show Preacher, where a man receives the word that created everything and people cannot help but obey it: the word of God is so powerful that when it comes out there is no gray area. When you have built everything up to this point, the word overpowers you and comes out with passion and conviction. None of us practice a style of speaking; that is the manifestation of the spirit. If you are a boring, dry teacher, you have some fire building to do in your spirit.

precepts.why:
An example of the fire. “If any man will hurt them, fire proceedeth out of their mouth, and devoureth their enemies.” It says the same thing as Jeremiah 5:14. There is a double meaning, but symbolically there is an authority and a judgment that comes through the word, and no doctrine will stand against it.

When we teach in Spanish-speaking countries, the words are so potent that the scripture says what it says and people are left dumbfounded, unable to say anything against it. In English everybody wants to argue semantics. But the word consumes and devours.

sense.text: Still dealing with fire, tying all the fire together. “His word was in mine heart as a burning fire”: you can’t keep it in; it has to be spoken. “Shut up in my bones, and I was weary with forbearing, and I could not stay.” I have to preach this word. The word ignites an inward compulsion so that you cannot remain silent.

precepts.why:
“Who may abide the day of his coming? and who shall stand when he appeareth? for he is like a refiner’s fire, and like fullers’ soap.” This speaks of Christ, because Christ is the word, the word made flesh. When you ignite that fire you are keeping the spirit of Christ in you, the one who knocks and comes in, in Revelation 3:20.

“He shall sit as a refiner and purifier of silver: and he shall purify the sons of Levi, and purge them as gold and silver.” The word of fire cleans, refines, purifies, purges, divides and discerns. It consumes because you are convicted.

The real reason many don’t give themselves wholly and don’t want that fire is that having it in your bones is like looking in a mirror and seeing the worst version of yourself, and then having to do something about it. Many would rather cover it with makeup than let the word go into the inward parts and find things out about them. The truth hurts, and the process is painful, but you can’t push it under the rug and expect the fire to do its work halfway. The transformative power of the word fills you with purpose, and this is not even our final form.

“Behold, the name of the Lord cometh from far, burning with his anger, and the burden thereof is heavy: his lips are full of indignation, and his tongue as a devouring fire.”

“The burden thereof is heavy” goes into what Jeremiah said when he could not bear it: to have that in you, it has to be put out. As 1 Timothy 4 says, when you truly give yourself wholly you will be saving others without even thinking about it. That is letting your light shine: a city cannot be hid. It takes no conscious effort, but it takes action.

“The voice of the Lord divideth the flames of fire.” That is another level of how powerful the word is. Imagine the little droplet of that power we receive from the word, and don’t think it won’t have its cleansing, driving effect, moving you and filling you with purpose even in the face of affliction.

“For the Lord thy God is a consuming fire, even a jealous God.” It uses these terms that we may understand. As you build yourself up to the point of wanting that fire, it will test you and purge all things even inside you. It cleanses into obedience and consumes the rebellious spirit. If you are a rebellious brother or sister, let this word in the way it has been built out here, step by step with application. You can’t just say fire, activate; you have to go through the parts.
“For our God is a consuming fire.” It says the same thing as Deuteronomy 4:24, reconfirming it: the God whose word burns in Jeremiah’s bones consumes.

“My heart was hot within me, while I was musing the fire burned: then spake I with my tongue.” To muse is to think upon many things. It happens inside first, in the mind, then into the bones and the spirit, and then it comes out of the mouth.

The musing goes into the meditation scriptures: giving yourself wholly, studying the doctrine, applying. It is the same as Luke 24:32, where their hearts burned within them.

“There appeared unto them cloven tongues like as of fire, and it sat upon each of them. And they were all filled with the Holy Ghost, and began to speak with other tongues, as the Spirit gave them utterance.”

This was a miracle, not gibberish. Read on and they were from different countries, each hearing in his own native language, with no translator needed. But the point is that the fire filled them with compulsion to do something. When the word is revealed, the spirit is kindled within, and that produces the passion and drive to speak the word: the utterance.

“For the word of God is quick, and powerful, and sharper than any twoedged sword, piercing even to the dividing asunder of soul and spirit.” When you muse on it and give yourself to it, it finds the wrong and the right. If you are not double minded and submit to it, letting it purge and purify, it activates something in you, and when obstacles come you know where to surrender to overcome them.

“And is a discerner of the thoughts and intents of the heart.” People say, that wasn’t my intent, as if that makes the action harmless, but the word reveals the intent. It pierces the inward man. It is the fire and the sword, an aggressive process designed to separate truth from error, fact from fiction, sin from what is good and holy.

“It is the spirit that quickeneth; the flesh profiteth nothing: the words that I speak unto you, they are spirit, and they are life.” That is how you get the fire, how you quicken and keep your spirit alive, the spiritual man or woman functioning.

The word of God is that fire, but unless you apply everything else from the beginning it won’t do what it needs to do in you. It burns inside so you desire to teach and share, and it devours any resistance against it. Even when the one you taught is not persuaded, it does not invalidate God’s word: they have been touched, either to repent or to be set firmer in their evil. It refines and purifies if you receive it in; it judges, discerns and gives life to the spirit.

That is the fire we all carry. The question is how big: a little ash with some warmth, or the roaring fire seen in how you move. It is not fleshly; it is zeal, the word inside you fully.
